title: Small businesses worry potential consumer pullback could cut into critical holiday sales
summary: The holiday shopping season is a critical money-making time for lots of retailers. But as retail sales point to a dip in consumer spending, small business owners worry a pullback by shoppers could…

image.caption: As the busy holiday shopping season gets underway, small business owners are worried consumers might cut back on spending this year, denting their sales. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

blocks.text: Business

The holiday shopping season is a critical money-making time for lots of retailers. But as retail sales point to a dip in consumer spending, small business owners worry a pullback by shoppers could dent their sales.
Pullback in spending biggest threat to holiday sales, according to survey of independent business owners
It's the most wonderful — and most important — time of the year for retailers like Kristi Wozniak: the holiday shopping season.
"It's very big," said Wozniak, owner and founder of Keylime Activewear in Sherwood Park, Alta. "We are in our busiest season right now for sure."
Wozniak says a quarter of her sales come from holiday shopping, with December being their busiest month.
But sales have been down recently compared to previous years, and she's worried that shoppers slowing their spending could cut into those critical holiday sales.
"Customers are definitely more cautious where they're spending their dollars," Wozniak said.
She's not alone. As small businesses struggle with tariffs and rising costs, some are worried that less spending by consumers this holiday season could deal another blow.
Kristi Wozniak, owner of Keylime Athletics, stands beside a sign advertising discounts at her storefront in Sherwood Park, Alta. (Submitted by Kristi Wozniak)

In a survey of 1,675 of its members from across the country, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business found that the holiday season is an important part of the financial outlook for four in 10 respondents. And 73 per cent of that group said a pullback in spending posed the biggest threat to holiday sales.

"In times of worsening affordability in the middle of a trade war, lack of consumer demand has actually been a key threat for many small businesses," said Ryan Mitton, the CFIB's director of legislative affairs for B.C.
And retail sales data from Statistics Canada shows consumers might, in fact, be trying to cut down on their spending.

Retail sales ticked up in September by 0.8 per cent — but that was driven mostly by a jump in how much consumers were spending at gas stations. And an early estimate for October forecasted a 1.5 per cent drop in retail sales.

items: Food and shelter have driven Canada's affordability crisis. Health care isn't far behind

blocks.text: Those figures give a "very weak kickoff point" for retail sales in the last quarter of the year, according to Michael Davenport, a senior economist with Oxford Economics.

He says high gas prices due to the war in Iran have been squeezing household budgets, while the weak job market and volatility in financial markets are weighing on consumer's confidence. And while consumer spending has been pretty resilient throughout the year despite some of those factors, he expects they'll cause Canadians to spend less in coming months.

items: Canadian economy lost 4,700 jobs in October as unemployment rate ticked up to 6.7%

blocks.text: "All of these factors are kind of coming together, we think, to lead to a bit of a slowdown in consumer spending growth towards the end of 2026 and early 2027."
Black Friday deal hunting with AI? What chatbots can miss
If holiday sales do take a hit, Wozniak says it could leave her with less cash to order new stock in the new year and force her to cut back some hours for staff.
"[If] we didn't make enough money for the previous season, now we're looking for cashflow options," Wozniak said.
She's stopped purchasing from some of her U.S. suppliers due to tariffs and to keep down costs related to shipping and the unfavorable exchange rate between the Canadian and U.S. dollar.
But rising manufacturing costs have still shrunken her profit margins in recent years, meaning she can't offer massive Black Friday discounts on clothing at Keylime like big box stores can.

blocks.text: Despite that, she's offering deals on gift cards and discounts that scale with the number of items shoppers buy, which she hopes will be enough to get buyers through the door — and spending some of their cash.
"We do want to attract the customer into the store," Wozniak said. "We try our hardest."
